title: Sensors Are Messengers
outcome: By the end, I can compare sensor readings while controlling where and when they are measured.
scenario: Two fictional light sensors disagree in a classroom. Compare them fairly rather than declaring one broken.
given: On the same shelf, simultaneous readings are A: 40,50,60 and B: 45,55,65 in declared toy light units.
Neither device has been compared with a trusted reference.

steps.label: Same shelf
steps.detail: Place both devices together and allow them to settle.

steps.label: Compare gaps
steps.detail: B minus A is 5, 5 and 5 units.

steps.label: Check a reference
steps.detail: A trusted reference is needed to decide which reading is closer.

explanation: A repeated difference of 5 supports investigating an offset between devices. Matching time and location removes two obvious comparison problems. It does not show which device is correct: both could have errors. Preserve paired readings instead of adjusting them silently.

counterfactual.change: Move only B into brighter light.
counterfactual.prediction: The next gap could change for reasons other than a difference in device accuracy.
counterfactual.reason: The comparison now changes location as well as device; there is no supplied reading from the new location.

student_task: Why can we calculate the earlier gap but not predict an exact new B reading?
teacher_answer: The earlier pairs give 5 each time. No measurement or light-response rule is given for B’s new location.
project_evidence: Save sorter measurements with device, location and time so unusual inputs can be checked before decisions.
limits: Three pairs do not prove an offset holds at every light level, nor identify the accurate device.
review_note: New fictional worked case reviewed against the weekly topic and reserved independent assessment. Keep that assessment separate; this picture is supported practice.
